ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Emerging adults aged 18 to 29 years and fluent in Italian were recruited through online snowball sampling on general social media platforms and were encouraged to share the invitation with peers from various social and occupational backgrounds to reach beyond university students.

> Adolescents aged 14 years or older with adequate knowledge of Italian were recruited between April and June 2026 in secondary schools in northern Italy.

> Parents gave informed consent online, and adolescents gave their assent; the questionnaires were completed anonymously on Qualtrics during school hours, in the presence of the researchers and a teacher, and participation was voluntary and uncompensated.

> Of 1,082 records, six were excluded for a completion time under 10 minutes or incomplete data, and eight because four participant codes appeared on two complete records each, which left 1,068 participants.

Ethics approval statement:

> Both studies aligned with the Ethical Code of the American Psychological Association and with the Declaration of Helsinki, and the Ethics Committee of the University of Milano-Bicocca approved all materials and procedures.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Mapping the Jingle–Jangle Jungle of Social-Learning Constructs: A Semantic–Psychometric Study of Mentalising, Epistemic Trust and Emotion Regulation
table.research_questions:
H1: Structural Fidelity
We hypothesise a statistically significant, positive correlation between the semantic similarity space (derived from language model embeddings) and the psychometric similarity space (derived from empirical item correlations). This will indicate that the linguistic content of social-learning questionnaires generally aligns with the empirical constructs they measure, establishing a baseline of structural fidelity.

H2: Measurement Mismatches (Jingle–Jangle Structure) (Exploratory)
Despite the general alignment predicted in H1, we expect the correspondence between semantic and psychometric similarity to be imperfect (r < 1.0), allowing the identification of systematic mismatches.
* H2a (Jingle-like structure): We will examine whether item pairs with high semantic similarity (top 20%) but low or non-significant psychometric correlation can be identified, consistent with distinct constructs using overlapping vocabulary.
* H2b (Jangle-like structure): We will examine whether item pairs with low semantic similarity (bottom 20%) but high psychometric correlation can be identified, consistent with theoretically distinct constructs that are empirically redundant.

H3: Associations with Personality Pathology
We hypothesise that disruptions in social learning are central to personality pathology.
* H3a: We expect differential patterns of association between item content and the SELF and INTER domains of the LPFS-BF, reflecting distinct aspects of social learning and personality functioning.
* H3b: We expect that items showing higher empirical redundancy across measures (jangle-like candidates) will show stronger associations with impairments in self and/or interpersonal functioning, as indexed by the SELF and INTER domains of the LPFS-BF, than items showing lower semantic and empirical overlap.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: Cross-sectional correlational design comparing two similarity matrices (Semantic vs. Psychometric) derived from 46 items (RFQY-13, ETMCQ, DERS-18). The study employs computational embedding models for the semantic matrix and observational survey data for the psychometric matrix, with matrix correspondence tested via Mantel tests and item validity assessed against the LPFS-BF.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to accessing the data
table.existing_data_explanation: The data for this study have already been collected as part of the larger study but have not yet been accessed for the purposes of this specific investigation.
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants were recruited via snowball sampling. Inclusion Criteria: Age 18–29 (emerging adults); fluent in Italian. Timeline: Data collection is complete. The data are currently stored on the Qualtrics platform and will be accessed for this specific analysis only after this pre-registration is published.
table.sample_size: We anticipate a final sample size of approximately N ≈ 800 emerging adults. The units of analysis are: Individual participants (for deriving the psychometric similarity space). Questionnaire items (k = 46; for the semantic-psychometric comparison).
table.sample_size_rationale:
The planned sample size (N ≈ 800) is determined by data availability within the parent study and is typical for item-level psychometric analyses in emerging adult samples. This sample size provides a stable estimation of item-level correlation matrices, which is the primary empirical input for the semantic–psychometric alignment analyses.

Given 46 questionnaire items, the analysis focuses on 1,035 unique item pairs. With N ≈ 800 participants, ordinal item correlations are expected to be estimated with high precision and low sampling variability, supporting reliable comparison between semantic and empirical similarity structures.

No formal power analysis was conducted, as the primary hypothesis concerns the correspondence between similarity matrices rather than mean-level effects or group differences, and inference is based on permutation testing (Mantel test) rather than parametric assumptions. The sample size is therefore considered adequate for detecting moderate matrix-level associations and for descriptive identification of semantic–psychometric mismatches.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection for the parent project is complete. We will include all valid responses available in the dataset at the moment of data extraction.
table.measured_variables:
Mentalising: Assessed using the Reflective Functioning Questionnaire for Youth (RFQY-13) (Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023). This 13-item self-report measure assesses the capacity to interpret behaviour in terms of mental states (e.g., "I know how I am feeling"). Items are rated on a Likert scale.

Epistemic Trust: Assessed using the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ) (Campbell et al., 2021). This 15-item measure assesses the individual's openness to social information. It comprises three subscales: Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity.

Emotion Regulation: Assessed using the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS-18) (Victor & Klonsky, 2016). This 18-item measure assesses difficulties in regulating negative emotions across domains such as clarity, awareness, and impulse control.

Personality Functioning: Assessed using the Level of Personality Functioning Scale – Brief Form (LPFS-BF) (Hutsebaut et al., 2016). This 12-item measure provides a global assessment of personality pathology severity, yielding two sub-scores: Self-Functioning: Identity and Self-Direction. Interpersonal Functioning: Empathy and Intimacy.
table.statistical_tests:
Analyses will be conducted at the item level to examine the correspondence between the semantic similarity of questionnaire items and their empirical associations in participant responses, and to explore the clinical relevance of semantic–psychometric mismatch.

Semantic similarity will be quantified using cosine similarity between multilingual sentence embeddings of item texts. Empirical similarity will be estimated from participant responses using ordinal item correlations (qgraph::cor_auto). Analyses will focus on the upper-triangular elements of the resulting item-by-item similarity matrices.

To test global semantic–psychometric alignment, we will compute the Pearson correlation between semantic and empirical similarity across all item pairs (1,035 pairs). Statistical significance will be evaluated using a Mantel test with 5,000 permutations, applied to distance-transformed matrices. Effect sizes and permutation-based p-values will be reported.

To characterise jingle–jangle structure, we will examine rank-based discrepancies between semantic and empirical similarity at the item-pair level. Item pairs showing the largest mismatches will be described as candidate jingle-like (high semantic, low empirical similarity) or jangle-like (low semantic, high empirical similarity). This analysis is descriptive and intended to illustrate the structure of mismatch rather than to define categorical thresholds.

To explore clinical relevance (H3), we will examine item-level associations with personality functioning (LPFS-BF). For H3b, we will formally test whether 'jangle-like' candidates exhibit stronger associations with Criterion A impairment than unique items using a Welch’s t-test on Fisher z-transformed correlations.
table.transformations: Fisher's z-transformation will be used for comparing correlation coefficients in the H3b analysis.
table.inference_criteria: We will use a standard alpha level of p < .05 for the Mantel test and for the H3b comparison of correlation strengths. The identification of H2 mismatch candidates is based on descriptive quintiles (top/bottom 20%).
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Participants will be excluded if they have incomplete data on any of the three primary questionnaires (RFQY-13, ETMCQ, DERS-18).
table.missing_data_handling: We will use listwise deletion for missing item responses.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 8650 columns across 56 data files.
#### Issues Identified

1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "items_46.csv", Column = "text_it", Issues = "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 66 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ..."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 56 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Emerging adults aged 18 to 29 years and fluent in Italian were recruited through online snowball sampling on general social media platforms and were encouraged to share the invitation with peers from various social and occupational backgrounds to reach beyond university students.
Adolescents aged 14 years or older with adequate knowledge of Italian were recruited between April and June 2026 in secondary schools in northern Italy.

Parents gave informed consent online, and adolescents gave their assent; the questionnaires were completed anonymously on Qualtrics during school hours, in the presence of the researchers and a teacher, and participation was voluntary and uncompensated.

Of 1,082 records, six were excluded for a completion time under 10 minutes or incomplete data, and eight because four participant codes appeared on two complete records each, which left 1,068 participants.

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. text.text: The item-level analyses were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/ka7d8).
text.formatted: The item-level analyses were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/ka7d8">https://osf.io/ka7d8</ref>).

text.text: The analysis code, the item and label texts, the embeddings, and the results are available at https://osf.io/4s63z.
text.formatted: The analysis code, the item and label texts, the embeddings, and the results are available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/4s63z">https://osf.io/4s63z</ref>.

text.text: Psychology has a measurement problem: different constructs often share the same name, and the same construct is measured under different names. Thorndike (1904) and Kelley (1927) described these as the jingle and jangle fallacies, one construct name used for measures of different constructs, or different construct names for measures of the same construct, and attributed them to a vague connection between psychological theory and its operationalization (Hanfstingl et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Psychology has a measurement problem: different constructs often share the same name, and the same construct is measured under different names. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Thorndike (1904)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kelley (1927)</ref> described these as the jingle and jangle fallacies, one construct name used for measures of different constructs, or different construct names for measures of the same construct, and attributed them to a vague connection between psychological theory and its operationalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hanfstingl et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Both rest on the assumption that a measure's name indicates what it contains (Elson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Both rest on the assumption that a measure's name indicates what it contains <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Elson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The assumption can be checked against two sources of evidence, the items a measure contains and the responses those items elicit, and both fallacies appear at both levels.

In the items, one name can cover different content: seven widely used depression scales together cover 52 symptoms, with low average overlap (Fried, 2017), seven self-report scales for obsessive-compulsive symptoms in youth share few of the 54 symptoms they assess (Visontay et al., 2019), and measures of general mental health in early and middle adolescence overlap little in content (Black et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In the items, one name can cover different content: seven widely used depression scales together cover 52 symptoms, with low average overlap <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fried, 2017)</ref>, seven self-report scales for obsessive-compulsive symptoms in youth share few of the 54 symptoms they assess <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Visontay et al., 2019)</ref>, and measures of general mental health in early and middle adolescence overlap little in content <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Black et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Different names can also cover the same content: grit items such as "I finish whatever I begin" and "I am a hard worker" are hard to tell apart from conscientiousness items such as "I carry out my plans" and "I work hard" (Henry et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Different names can also cover the same content: grit items such as "I finish whatever I begin" and "I am a hard worker" are hard to tell apart from conscientiousness items such as "I carry out my plans" and "I work hard" <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Henry et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In participants' responses, measures with different names can be nearly redundant: job satisfaction and organizational commitment, conceptually distinct, correlated .91 once corrected for measurement error (Le et al., 2010), and grit correlated .84 with conscientiousness after the same correction (Credé et al., 2017).

text.text: Measures administered under one name can also reflect more than one construct: measures of adolescent autonomy in the family reflected two distinct dimensions (Van Petegem et al., 2013).

text.text: When the assumption fails, subscales may be entered as separate predictors in the same models, differences between them may receive a clinical interpretation, and researchers and reviews may group them under headings that assume they are distinct, when they may not be.

Current review and meta-analytic methods do not detect these fallacies (Hanfstingl et al., 2024), since studies are selected and grouped by the construct names they report: a jingle pools measures of different constructs under one heading, and a jangle keeps measures of the same construct under separate ones. Wulff and Mata (2025) highlight the resulting taxonomic incommensurability: findings obtained under different construct taxonomies are difficult to compare and integrate.
text.formatted: Current review and meta-analytic methods do not detect these fallacies <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hanfstingl et al., 2024)</ref>, since studies are selected and grouped by the construct names they report: a jingle pools measures of different constructs under one heading, and a jangle keeps measures of the same construct under separate ones. <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Wulff and Mata (2025)</ref> highlight the resulting taxonomic incommensurability: findings obtained under different construct taxonomies are difficult to compare and integrate.

text.text: We argue that the problem weighs particularly on clinical psychology, a discipline concerned with meaning.
People communicate their emotions, intentions, and patterns of behavior through language, and clinicians rely on these accounts to understand distress and adaptive functioning.
Self-report questionnaires, the most widely used instruments in clinical and developmental research, are themselves made of language.
Each item is a condensed description of a psychological state or tendency, and participants' responses indicate how they understood and endorsed that description (Schwarz, 1999).
text.formatted: Each item is a condensed description of a psychological state or tendency, and participants' responses indicate how they understood and endorsed that description <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Schwarz, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: The validity of a measure therefore depends on the meaning of its wording as well as on its statistical properties (Borsboom et al., 2004; Maul, 2017).
text.formatted: The validity of a measure therefore depends on the meaning of its wording as well as on its statistical properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Borsboom et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Maul, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The construct name is language too: it says what the items are taken to measure, and it is the basis on which findings obtained with different instruments are compared and grouped in reviews and meta-analyses.
Construct names and items thus stand at the two ends of the connection between theory and operationalization, and both can be compared as language.
The problem might be particularly evident for constructs that theory describes as interdependent, and we take the mentalizing framework as a case study.

Mentalizing is the capacity to understand the self and others in terms of intentional mental states, such as feelings, desires, wishes, attitudes, and goals (Bateman & Fonagy, 2016; Luyten et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Mentalizing is the capacity to understand the self and others in terms of intentional mental states, such as feelings, desires, wishes, attitudes, and goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bateman & Fonagy, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Luyten et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It is linked to epistemic trust (ET), an individual's willingness to consider new knowledge from another person as trustworthy, generalizable, and relevant to the self (Fonagy & Allison, 2014), which is both facilitated by and facilitates mentalizing (Luyten et al., 2020).
text.formatted: It is linked to epistemic trust (ET), an individual's willingness to consider new knowledge from another person as trustworthy, generalizable, and relevant to the self <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fonagy & Allison, 2014)</ref>, which is both facilitated by and facilitates mentalizing <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Luyten et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The experience of having one's own subjectivity understood, of being mentalized, is thought to open epistemic trust and, with it, the possibility of learning from social communication (Fonagy & Allison, 2014).
text.formatted: The experience of having one's own subjectivity understood, of being mentalized, is thought to open epistemic trust and, with it, the possibility of learning from social communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fonagy & Allison, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Mentalizing and emotion regulation are linked in a circular way: stress and arousal shift mentalizing from controlled to automatic and often biased modes (Luyten et al., 2020), and "mentalizing difficulties lead to affect dysregulation, which in turn further disrupts mentalizing" (Fonagy et al., 2017, p. 4).

text.text: Together, these capacities form a social learning system through which individuals acquire and update knowledge about themselves and the social world in communication with trusted others, and disruptions of this system have been proposed to underlie a general vulnerability to psychopathology, captured by the p-factor, and personality pathology (Fonagy et al., 2017; Luyten et al., 2020).

text.text: Both fallacies, at both levels, are visible in this domain.

Within the framework itself, mentalizing is described as "an umbrella concept that overlaps with a range of constructs and capacities, such as Theory of Mind (ToM), mindfulness, perspective taking, and empathy" (Luyten et al., 2020, p. 300).
text.formatted: Within the framework itself, mentalizing is described as "an umbrella concept that overlaps with a range of constructs and capacities, such as Theory of Mind (ToM), mindfulness, perspective taking, and empathy" <ref type="bibr">(Luyten et al., 2020, p. 300)</ref>.

text.text: In the content of the measures, one construct name covers many instruments: a systematic review of questionnaire, interview, and text-coding measures of mentalizing in adults identified 57 instruments, and no two overlapped completely on the 18 components, 17 dimensions of mentalizing, and the relational context of the framework used to describe them (Hawksdale et al., 2025); likewise, tasks that share the construct name theory of mind measure different processes (Quesque & Rossetti, 2020).

text.text: Different construct names also cover the same items: the same review included among measures of mentalizing, although with a differing focus, the Lack of Emotional Clarity and Awareness subscales of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (Gratz & Roemer, 2004; Hawksdale et al., 2025, Table  10), so the same items are given the construct name of emotion regulation in one literature and of mentalizing in another.

text.text: In participants' responses, theory of mind tasks correlate weakly with each other (Warnell & Redcay, 2019), and in a meta-analysis of the correlations among ten commonly measured emotion regulation strategies, none of the theory-based structural models fitted the data (Naragon-Gainey et al., 2017).

text.text: Current reporting practices allow overlap of this kind to go undetected (Flake & Fried, 2020).
text.formatted: Current reporting practices allow overlap of this kind to go undetected <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Flake & Fried, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Because the interdependence of the three capacities is posited at the level of construct names, and each construct is measured by a pool of items from a separate instrument and told apart mainly by the construct names of its subscales, an association between two such measures can have three sources: the words in which construct names and items are written, the instruments through which the constructs are observed, and the interdependence of the capacities themselves.
Semantic embeddings offer a way to compare construct names and items directly.

Items, scales, and construct names are represented as vectors in a shared space, in which proximity reflects use in similar linguistic contexts, so that the similarity between two descriptions becomes measurable and reproducible (Hussain et al., 2024; Larsen & Bong, 2016; Rosenbusch et al., 2020). Wulff and Mata (2025) used such a space for several thousand personality items and the scales and construct names that organize them: semantic similarity predicted the empirical associations between items and between scales, and the space was used to flag candidate jingle and jangle fallacies and to propose a taxonomy with fewer constructs.

text.text: The authors present these tools as an aid to expert deliberation (Wulff & Mata, 2025 , 2026) and caution that semantically similar constructs should not always be treated as identical (Wulff & Mata, 2026, p. 63).

text.text: Part of this judgment rests on participants' responses: of the ten criteria proposed by Lawson and Robins (2021) to establish whether two constructs are siblings, closely related and still distinct, four are empirical and concern the observed nomological networks, the association between the measures, a common general factor, and incremental validity (see also Blötner, 2025).

text.text: Two questions remain open.
First, does the agreement between items and participants' responses hold across questionnaires as well as within them?

Wulff and Mata (2025) validated the semantic space against correlations collected in separate samples, one for each inventory, and used a sample that answered several inventories only to fine-tune the model.
Items from the same questionnaire share authors, format, response scale, and often wording, so part of their correlation may come from the questionnaire itself.
Separating this part requires the same participants to answer all the questionnaires, which is also the design required by the empirical criteria of Lawson and Robins (2021).
text.formatted: Separating this part requires the same participants to answer all the questionnaires, which is also the design required by the empirical criteria of <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lawson and Robins (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Second, are the candidate fallacies flagged from the text confirmed by participants' responses?
Wulff and Mata (2025) examined them by inspecting their items, without testing them against the responses of participants who completed both measures.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Wulff and Mata (2025)</ref> examined them by inspecting their items, without testing them against the responses of participants who completed both measures.

text.text: These questions are especially pressing in a domain like clinical psychology. Wulff and Mata (2025) worked with broad personality inventories covering many distinct traits.
text.formatted: These questions are especially pressing in a domain like clinical psychology. <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Wulff and Mata (2025)</ref> worked with broad personality inventories covering many distinct traits.

text.text: Here, a few closely related constructs are measured with questionnaires that often share stems and response formats, so that items written for different constructs can be similar in wording, and part of their correlation may come from the questionnaires.
If a theoretical construct is the territory, its construct name, its items, and participants' responses are three maps of it.
Building on this evidence, the present study asks whether these maps converge in measures of mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation.

In two large samples of emerging adults and adolescents who completed the Reflective Functioning Questionnaire for Youth (RFQY-13; Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023), the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ; Campbell et al., 2021), and the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale-Short Form (DERS-SF; Kaufman et al., 2016), we compared the construct names and items of their 11 subscales with participants' responses, with three specific aims.
text.formatted: In two large samples of emerging adults and adolescents who completed the Reflective Functioning Questionnaire for Youth <ref type="bibr">(RFQY-13;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023)</ref>, the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Campbell et al., 2021)</ref>, and the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale-Short Form (DERS-SF; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kaufman et al., 2016)</ref>, we compared the construct names and items of their 11 subscales with participants' responses, with three specific aims.

text.text: First (Aim 1), we asked whether construct names identify their items, that is, whether the items of each subscale are semantically closer to its own construct name than to the construct names of the other subscales.

Second (Aim 2), we asked whether the semantic similarity between items predicts the correlation between participants' responses to them, at the level of items and of subscales, and whether this holds both within and across questionnaires.

Third (Aim 3), we asked whether participants' responses follow construct names or items: whether the correlations between subscales are more strongly associated with the similarity of their construct names or with the similarity of their items, over all pairs and for the candidate jingle and jangle fallacies flagged from text with an adaptation of the criterion of Wulff and Mata (2025).
text.formatted: Third (Aim 3), we asked whether participants' responses follow construct names or items: whether the correlations between subscales are more strongly associated with the similarity of their construct names or with the similarity of their items, over all pairs and for the candidate jingle and jangle fallacies flagged from text with an adaptation of the criterion of <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Wulff and Mata (2025)</ref>.

text.text: We expected the semantic similarity between two items to be positively associated with the correlation between participants' responses to them (H1), and planned to describe the pairs at which the two disagree as candidate jingle-like and jangle-like pairs (H2).

Because disruptions of social learning are hypothesized to underlie personality pathology, we also expected items to differ in their associations with the self and interpersonal domains of personality functioning (H3a), and items in jangle-like pairs to be more strongly associated with impairment than items without overlap (H3b).

Emerging adults aged 18 to 29 years and fluent in Italian were recruited through online snowball sampling on general social media platforms and were encouraged to share the invitation with peers from various social and occupational backgrounds to reach beyond university students.
After giving informed consent online, they completed a 30-minute questionnaire on Qualtrics, with CAPTCHA verification at entry; participation was voluntary and uncompensated.
Sample size was not set by a power analysis.

The data had been collected within a larger survey and had not been accessed when the study was registered; the registration anticipated approximately 800 participants and the inclusion of all valid responses available at extraction.

Of 1,470 participants with a completion time of at least 10 minutes, 1,167 (79.4%) had complete data on the three questionnaires and were retained as registered, so that every correlation is estimated on the same respondents.
The excluded participants differed negligibly from the included ones on the RFQY-13 and ETMCQ subscales they had completed, except for a small difference on Certainty (d = -0.23).
Mean age was 24.22 years (SD = 2.77).
Sex assigned at birth was female for 72.1%; gender identity was female for 68.6%, male for 27.8%, and non-binary or another identity for 3.6%.
Most described themselves as heterosexual (74.5%), 96.3% were born in Italy, 59.1% were students, and 65.1% held a university degree.
The adolescent sample was not part of the registration and was analyzed with the same code.
Adolescents aged 14 years or older with adequate knowledge of Italian were recruited between April and June 2026 in secondary schools in northern Italy.

Parents gave informed consent online, and adolescents gave their assent; the questionnaires were completed anonymously on Qualtrics during school hours, in the presence of the researchers and a teacher, and participation was voluntary and uncompensated.

Of 1,082 records, six were excluded for a completion time under 10 minutes or incomplete data, and eight because four participant codes appeared on two complete records each, which left 1,068 participants.
Mean age was 16.71 years (SD = 1.28, range 14 to 20), across the five years of secondary school.
Sex assigned at birth was female for 67.0%; gender identity was female for 65.6%, male for 32.8%, and non-binary, another identity, or not reported for 1.7%; 96.3% were born in Italy.
The LPFS-BF was administered in some schools only and was completed by 661 participants, on whom the analyses involving the external criterion are based.

Both studies aligned with the Ethical Code of the American Psychological Association and with the Declaration of Helsinki, and the Ethics Committee of the University of Milano-Bicocca approved all materials and procedures.
The two samples completed the same Italian versions of the instruments.

The Reflective Functioning Questionnaire for Youth (RFQY-13; Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023) yields two subscales, Uncertainty about mental states (7 items) and Certainty about mental states (6 items), and was administered on a 7-point scale.
Epistemic trust.

The Epistemic Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ; Campbell et al., 2021; Liotti et al., 2023; Milesi et al., 2024) has 15 items rated on a 7-point scale and three subscales of five items: Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity.

As registered, item associations were estimated as polychoric correlations (cor_auto in qgraph); subscale associations were the Pearson correlations among subscale scores, as in Wulff and Mata (2025).

text.text: Comparisons with semantic similarity use absolute correlations.
Two similarity matrices were compared with the Pearson correlation over their pairs and tested with one-sided permutation (Mantel) tests.

H1 is the confirmatory test; the other pvalues are uncorrected, and conclusions rest on effects that recur in both samples, which were analyzed separately with the same code and settings and were neither pooled nor compared statistically.
Aim 1.

For each subscale, we computed the cosine between its items and each of the 11 construct names and report the z score and rank of its own construct name, as in Wulff and Mata (2025), tested against random reassignment of construct names to subscales.
Aim 2.

In this contribution, we aimed to examine whether construct names, items, and participants' responses tell the same story about measures of mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation, three capacities that theory describes as interdependent and that are measured with separate questionnaires.

The three maps only partially converged, and in the same way in emerging adults and in adolescents: construct names rarely identified their own items, participants' responses followed the items, more closely within than across questionnaires, and where names and items disagreed about a pair of subscales, the responses sided with the items.
We take the three aims in turn, then ask what the pattern means for the three capacities, and finally what it means beyond them.
Only four of the 11 construct names were the closest description of their own items, and the name that described most subscales best was Lack of emotional clarity.
The second finding explains the first.

Across the three questionnaires most items describe one experience, not knowing what one feels, thinks, or why one acts, and a name that states this experience fits them better than names such as Epistemic mistrust or Limited access to emotion regulation strategies, which state a theoretical construct and say little about the content of its items.

This is a direct instance of the assumption on which jingle and jangle fallacies rest, that the name of a measure tells what it contains (Elson et al., 2023), and it departs from the close alignment between construct names and scale content found for personality inventories (Wulff & Mata, 2025, p. 947).

text.text: Part of the gap lies in the names as input to a language model: they are short technical phrases, rare in general text, whose parts are related in ways a cosine does not express (Ciapparelli et al., 2025; Günther et al., 2019), and a phrase without context yields a less reliable representation than one drawn from its uses (Cassani et al., 2023).

text.text: For a reader of this literature, the practical point is simple: an argument built on construct names is built on the least reliable of the three maps.

The semantic similarity of two items predicted how strongly participants' responses to them were associated, as registered, which extends the validation of semantic embeddings in personality (Hussain et al., 2024; Wulff & Mata, 2025) to clinical constructs measured in Italian.

text.text: What the design adds is the comparison across questionnaires, which separate samples for each inventory could not provide, and here the correspondence was clearly lower.

This is what the multitrait-multimethod logic anticipates when the questionnaire acts as a method (Campbell & Fiske, 1959): items written for the same instrument share authors, format, response scale, and often wording, and part of their agreement, in text as in responses, comes from the instrument.
text.formatted: This is what the multitrait-multimethod logic anticipates when the questionnaire acts as a method <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959)</ref>: items written for the same instrument share authors, format, response scale, and often wording, and part of their agreement, in text as in responses, comes from the instrument.

text.text: Thus, in the semantic map the items are organized by instrument; in the response map they are organized by whether they describe a difficulty or a capacity, and the items describing difficulties from the three questionnaires occupy one region regardless of the instrument they come from.

The text of the items is therefore a useful guide to how people will answer, and the two things it does not see are the method effect of the instrument and the axis along which the responses are actually organized.

A second bound lies in what the two spaces represent: semantic models represent meaning at the level of a population of speakers (Günther et al., 2019), whereas a response records how one person read and endorsed a description (Schwarz, 1999), so the two can agree only as far as participants read the items alike.

text.text: Where names and items disagreed about a pair of subscales, participants' responses followed the items in every pair within an instrument.
The three jingles were pairs of subscales named on a common template, a choice often made precisely to tell subscales apart, and their responses were nearly independent.

The two jangles within the DERS-SF were pairs whose names are distant and whose items share a stem, and their responses were among the most correlated of all, giving no support to the distinction the names suggest; by the empirical criteria of Lawson and Robins (2021), such pairs are candidates for siblings or for a single construct, a judgment that would also require evidence on their nomological networks and incremental validity.

text.text: Second, the experience of not knowing what one feels sits at the center of the three instruments under three construct names.

RFQY-13 Uncertainty and DERS-SF Clarity both describe it, one item of each is almost the same sentence, and their responses were closely related; the ETMCQ Mistrust item most associated with impaired personality functioning describes feeling that others do not understand what one wants or needs.

The mentalizing approach places this experience under the self-oriented and affective poles of mentalizing (Fonagy & Luyten, 2009), research on emotion regulation calls it a lack of clarity (Gratz & Roemer, 2004), a review of mentalizing measures counts the DERS Clarity and Awareness subscales among them (Hawksdale et al., 2025), and in the theory the experience of having one's own mind understood is what opens epistemic trust (Fonagy & Allison, 2014).

text.text: When the three questionnaires correlate, then, part of the correlation is this one experience described three times, and part is a general factor of difficulty that the response map makes visible, in which items from the three instruments form one region; whether that factor is the general vulnerability that disruptions of social learning are proposed to underlie (Fonagy et al., 2017; Luyten et al., 2020) or the direction in which the items are worded cannot be told apart in these data.

text.text: The interdependence the theory proposes may well be real, but with these instruments it cannot be separated from shared wording and shared method, and what theory says about each construct applies only in part to what its items measure.
Third, the capacities stand apart.

Epistemic trust, Certainty about mental states, and emotional awareness occupied their own regions of the response map, away from the difficulties, and were unrelated or weakly related to personality functioning in both samples, with the caveat that DERS-SF Awareness behaved differently in the adolescents (Mancinelli et al., 2024).

text.text: In these instruments the social learning system is measured almost entirely from its deficit side, and the capacities that the theory describes as its working state are measured by subscales that do not covary with the rest.
For the researcher and the clinician in this field, the consequences are tangible.

High scores on Uncertainty, Clarity, and Mistrust add less independent evidence than the names of three questionnaires suggest, and reading the items a patient endorsed turns the scores back into the clinical material they summarize.
Studies that enter these subscales as separate predictors should expect their shared variance to be large and should avoid "mindlessly partialing out shared variance" (Lawson & Robins, 2021, p. 359).
text.formatted: Studies that enter these subscales as separate predictors should expect their shared variance to be large and should avoid "mindlessly partialing out shared variance" <ref type="bibr">(Lawson & Robins, 2021, p. 359)</ref>.

text.text: Validation studies of a new measure of any of the three capacities would gain from reporting its correlations with the instruments of the other two traditions, which are likely to be administered alongside it.
Mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation are one case.
What the case shows is a method and an order of reliability.

Construct names, items, and participants' responses are three descriptions of the same constructs, and they can be compared in the same participants; when they are, the items are the description that the responses follow, the instrument sets the limit of that correspondence, and the names are the description to trust least. Wulff and Mata (2025) call the difficulty of comparing findings across construct taxonomies taxonomic incommensurability, a term Kuhn (1962) applied to scientific theories; here it arises in the words in which names and items are written and in the instruments through which the constructs are observed, and only what remains once both are accounted for can be attributed to the constructs themselves.

text.text: For research and reviews, the overlap between two measures is best checked through their items and participants' responses before they are combined, compared, or entered in the same model; coding studies by the content of their items (Hawksdale et al., 2025) and screening candidate groupings with semantic tools (Rosenbusch et al., 2020; Wulff & Mata, 2026) would make such decisions explicit, and such decisions are rarely reported (Flake & Fried, 2020).

Separating shared method from shared capacity, finally, requires observing the constructs with methods other than self-report, such as interviews scored for reflective functioning, behavioral tasks, and informant reports (Campbell & Fiske, 1959).

text.text: All measures were single-occasion self-reports.
A theoretical construct is known through three descriptions: the name it is given, the items written to measure it, and the answers people give to those items.
The present study compared the three in the same participants and found that they converged only in part.

Participants' responses followed the items, the instrument bounded that correspondence, and the names, the description on which theories are written and literatures are organized, were the least reliable of the three.

In measures of mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation, the interdependence that theory proposes among the three capacities could not be separated from the experience their items share and from the questionnaires through which they are observed.

The same comparison can be made wherever constructs theorized as related are measured with separate instruments, and until it is made, what theory says about a construct applies only in part to what its items measure.

The registered quintile rule yielded 8 jingle-like and 3 jangle-like item pairs in the emerging adults, and 20 jingle-like and 2 jangle-like pairs in the adolescents; six of the adolescent jingle-like pairs and both jangle-like pairs were also found in the emerging adults.

Five of the six shared jingle-like pairs joined the RFQY-13 Certainty item stating that one usually knows exactly what other people are thinking with Trust and Credulity items of the ETMCQ, and the sixth joined a Trust and a Mistrust item.
In the adolescents, 13 of the 20 jinglelike pairs involved the three reverse-keyed DERS-SF Awareness items.

The jangle-like pairs found in both samples joined two Mistrust items of the ETMCQ with little shared vocabulary, a mismatch between wording and responses within one subscale, and an RFQY-13 Uncertainty item about not knowing why one acts as one does with the DERS-SF Strategies item about expecting to remain upset for a long time; in the emerging adults the first Mistrust item also formed a jangle-like pair with the same DERS-SF item.
The four items involved in jangle-like pairs were the same in the two samples.

As described by H3a, the subscales differed in their patterns of association with the two domains of the LPFS-BF, and the items of most subscales were more strongly associated with the Self than with the Interpersonal domain.

The highest mean absolute correlations were those of DERS-SF Clarity (.58 with Self and .41 with Interpersonal), Strategies (.55 and .38), and RFQY-13 Uncertainty (.48 and .37) in the emerging adults, and of DERS-SF Clarity (.52 and .39), Goals (.52 and .41), and Strategies (.51 and .43) in the adolescents.

The lowest were those of RFQY-13 Certainty (.03 and .06) and ETMCQ Trust (.05 and .07) in the emerging adults, and of DERS-SF Awareness (.01 and .03), ETMCQ Trust (.09 and .08), and RFQY-13 Certainty (.11 and .04) in the adolescents.
ETMCQ Mistrust and Credulity were equally associated with the two domains.

The Mistrust items differed among themselves, from the item about feeling that others do not understand what one wants or needs (.47 and .48 with Self) to the item about preferring to search the internet over asking other people (.22 and .15).
Certainty and Uncertainty about mental states are two separate scales in these data, and only one of them measures personality impairment.

Their names are among the most similar of the 55 pairs, their items describe different things, one's own feelings and other people's minds(Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023), their responses were nearly independent, and they differed sharply in their relation to personality functioning: Uncertainty was among the subscales most associated with the Self domain, Certainty showed no linear association with either domain, which leaves open the curvilinear relation that the hypermentalizing reading would predict for excessive certainty.
